Course Description
MC 451—Research Methods in Mass Media introduces students to core research methodologies used in mass communication. Through this course, students will explore quantitative and qualitative research methods, including surveys, experimental designs, content analysis, and in-depth interviews. The course emphasizes development of skills necessary for the design, execution, and presentation of research studies while engaging with professional and ethical principles that guide mass communication research.

Q: Do I need to download the textbook?
A: No, it’s optional. You can access course readings through the library or online sources.
Q: Can I use Excel instead of R?
A: Yes, Excel works for basic analysis. R is recommended for more complex projects.
Q: What if I already use a note-taking app?
A: Obsidian is recommended but optional. The course works with Notion, OneNote, or even physical notebooks.
Q: Where do I turn in my work?
A: Save deliverables in your Liaison_Vault under 03_Project/. Dr. Leith will collect via email or learning management system.
Q: Can I work with others?
A: Absolutely! Pair programming and collaborative analysis are encouraged. Document who contributed what.
Q: What if I fall behind?
A: Reach out to Dr. Leith early. The phases are structured but flexible—we can adjust timelines if needed.
Q: Are there textbooks or readings?
A: Course readings will be posted in each phase. Check Phase 1 for the syllabus.

title: 🎯 Phase V: The Publisher
text:
Phase 5 Content & Activities

Activity 1: Craft Your Story (Week 11)
Before making slides, nail your narrative:

Identify your key insights - Which 2-3 findings matter most?
Create an outline - How do you guide your audience through the data?
Add “So what?” - For each finding, explain why it matters

Outline Template:
# Research Story Outline

## Hook (30 seconds)
[What question were we answering? Why does it matter?]

## Context (1-2 minutes)
[Brief background: who cares, what was the challenge?]

## The Findings (3-4 minutes)
### Finding 1: [Headline]
- Data point 1
- Data point 2
- **So what?** [Why does this matter? What should we do?]

### Finding 2: [Headline]
- Data point 1
- Data point 2
- **So what?** [Implications]

### Finding 3: [Headline]
- Data point 1
- Data point 2
- **So what?** [Action items]

## Limitations (1 minute)
[What are we uncertain about?]

## Next Steps (1-2 minutes)
[What should happen next?]
Create: 03_Project/04_Drafts/Story_Outline.md


Activity 2: Create a Slide Deck or Brief (Week 12)
Option A: Slide Deck (for live presentation) - Title slide with question - 1 context slide - 2-3 finding slides with visualizations - 1 limitations slide - 1 next steps/call-to-action slide - Total: 7-8 slides (aim for 1-2 minutes per slide)
Option B: One-Page Brief (for email/sharing) - Header with research question - 3-4 key findings with visual - Brief interpretation - Limitations (small print) - Contact + next steps
Design Tips: - ✅ One major idea per slide - ✅ Large, readable fonts (18pt minimum) - ✅ Colors that support understanding (not decoration) - ✅ Real data visuals (your actual charts/tables) - ✅ Simple, clean layouts - ❌ Avoid: dense text, clip art, too many colors
Tools: - Google Slides (free, easy sharing) - PowerPoint (familiar, flexible) - Keynote (Apple, polished) - Canva (beautiful templates) - Quarto (reproducible, code-based)
Create: 03_Project/04_Drafts/Presentation_Deck.pdf or Brief.pdf


Activity 3: Translate for Your Audience (Week 12)
Different audiences, different messages:
For Executives: - Bottom line: What’s the recommendation? - Impact: What does this mean for our goals? - Minimize jargon; focus on action
For Data Scientists: - Methodology: How did you approach this? - Limitations: What aren’t we capturing? - Code & details available if needed
For General Audience: - Story: What happened and why does it matter? - Visuals: Show don’t tell - Plain language: Avoid stats jargon
Create: Brief version (1-2 sentences) of each finding for different audiences in your outline.


Activity 4: Presentation & Reflection (Week 13)
Presentation Options: - In-class presentation (5-10 minutes) - Recorded video (3-5 minutes) - Written report with visuals - Poster presentation (if poster session)
Before presenting: 1. Rehearse with a peer - Get feedback 2. Time yourself - Stay within limits 3. Check visuals - Do all graphs display correctly? 4. Practice Q&A - What might people ask?
After presenting: 1. Capture feedback - What questions did people ask? 2. Note surprises - What did people react to most? 3. Reflect in journal - What would you do differently next time?

Key Concepts

Variable Types
Numeric - Numbers you can do math with (age, score, count)
Categorical - Limited set of categories (gender, region, type)
Text/String - Free-form text (name, comment, description)
Date - Time-based (2024-01-15)
Boolean - True/False or Yes/No


Measurement Scales
Nominal - Categories with no order (blue, red, green)
Ordinal - Ranked categories (low, medium, high)
Interval - Numbers with equal spacing (temperature in°C)
Ratio - Numbers with true zero (height, weight, age)

Repositories (Repos)

section: Step 4: Clone a Repository (Get It on Your Computer)
text:
Step 4: Clone a Repository (Get It on Your Computer)

4.1 Install Git
To work with repositories on your computer, you need Git (the tool GitHub uses).
Windows: 1. Download Git from git-scm.com 2. Run the installer and follow default options 3. Restart your computer
Mac: 1. Download Git from git-scm.com or use Homebrew 2. Open Terminal and run: brew install git
Linux: Open Terminal and run:
sudo apt-get install git


4.2 Clone Your First Repository

Go to your hello-world repository on GitHub
Click the green “Code” button
Copy the HTTPS URL (should look like https://github.com/yourusername/hello-world.git)
Open Terminal (Mac/Linux) or PowerShell (Windows)
Navigate to where you want to store your repository:
cd Documents
Clone the repository:
git clone https://github.com/yourusername/hello-world.git
Enter the repository folder:
cd hello-world

Congratulations! You now have a copy of your repository on your computer.

title: Getting Started with GitHub
text:
Step 5: Make Your First Commit

5.1 Edit Your README

Open the folder hello-world on your computer
Find the file README.md and open it in a text editor (Notepad, VS Code, etc.)
Add some content:

# Hello World

This is my first GitHub repository.

## About Me
- I'm a Communication Liaison
- I'm learning research methods
- I'm excited to collaborate

## Goals
- Master data analysis
- Tell stories with data
- Connect technical and creative teams

Save the file



5.2 Push Changes to GitHub
Back in Terminal/PowerShell, run these commands:
# Stage your changes (tell Git which files to save)
git add README.md

# Commit your changes (save them locally with a message)
git commit -m "Update README with introduction"

# Push changes to GitHub (send them to the website)
git push
Go back to GitHub.com, refresh your hello-world repository page, and you’ll see your updated README!

Term
Meaning

A folder that stores your project and its history

A saved version of your work with a message describing what changed

Download changes from GitHub to your computer

title: Getting Started with GitHub
text:
Step 7: Best Practices

1. Use Clear Commit Messages
Bad: “Update stuff” or “Fix”
Good: “Add data analysis section to README” or “Fix typo in methods section”


2. Commit Often
Make commits when you complete a logical task, not just once per day.


3. Keep Your README Updated
Your README is the first impression. Keep it current and clear.


4. Make It Public
For this course, make your repository public so I can see your work. You can always make it private later for sensitive projects.


5. Use Meaningful Repository Names
Bad: project or stuff
Good: mc451-research-analysis or data-storytelling-project

title: Getting Started with GitHub
text:
Step 8: Troubleshooting

“Permission denied” Error
If you see Permission denied (publickey), you need to set up SSH authentication. For now, use HTTPS (which you’re already doing). Later, GitHub has tutorials to set up SSH if needed.


Changes Not Appearing on GitHub
Make sure you: 1. ✅ Used git add to stage files 2. ✅ Used git commit -m "message" to commit 3. ✅ Used git push to push to GitHub
All three steps are necessary!


How to Undo a Commit
If you made a mistake, run:
git log  # See your commit history
git revert HEAD  # Undo the last commit

Common First-Time Issues

“Command not found: R”
Problem: Your computer doesn’t recognize the R command.
Solution: - Try restarting your computer after installation - Check that R installed correctly (reinstall if needed) - On Mac/Linux, you may need to use /usr/bin/R instead


RStudio Opens But Doesn’t Find R
Problem: RStudio says “R not found” when you open it.
Solution: 1. Make sure you installed R first (before RStudio) 2. In RStudio, go to Tools → Global Options → General 3. Under “R sessions”, check the “R home directory” 4. If empty, browse to your R installation folder and select it 5. Click “OK”


“Error: Could not find function”

Solution: You need to load the package first. Run:
library(ggplot2)  # or whichever package you need

Solution: 1. Press Escape to stop it 2. Try installing from a different CRAN mirror:
install.packages("tidyverse", repos="https://cloud.r-project.org")


“Permission denied” Error (Mac/Linux)

Solution: Try:
Sys.which("R")  # Check where R is installed

title: Chapter 1: The Science of Storytelling
text:
Welcome to the SIM Lab. If you are reading this, you likely identify as a “creative.” You are a writer, a designer, a strategist, or a storyteller. You might feel that “research” is the opposite of what you do—a cold, clinical practice performed by people in lab coats who care more about numbers than people.
This chapter exists to dismantle that belief. Research is not the enemy of creativity; it is the engine of it. At its core, research is simply a specialized, rigorous form of the storytelling you are already passionate about. To be a great researcher, you must first understand the neuroscience of narrative.

title: Chapter 1: The Science of Storytelling
text:
Welcome to the SIM Lab. If you are reading this, you likely identify as a “creative.” You are a writer, a designer, a strategist, or a storyteller. You might feel that “research” is the opposite of what you do—a cold, clinical practice performed by people in lab coats who care more about numbers than people.
This chapter exists to dismantle that belief. Research is not the enemy of creativity; it is the engine of it. At its core, research is simply a specialized, rigorous form of the storytelling you are already passionate about. To be a great researcher, you must first understand the neuroscience of narrative.

title: Chapter 1: The Science of Storytelling
section: 1.1 Theoretical Foundation: The Brain as a Story Processor
text:
1.1 Theoretical Foundation: The Brain as a Story Processor
We begin not with statistics, but with neuroscience. In The Science of Storytelling, Will Storr argues that the human brain is not a logic processor, but a “story processor”. This fundamental insight transforms how we approach both creative work and scientific inquiry.

The Control-Seeking Brain
The brain’s primary evolutionary function is to control its environment to ensure survival. To do this, it builds internal models—hallucinations, essentially—of the world around us. We walk into a room and our brain instantly predicts:

The physics of the floor beneath our feet
The social dynamics of the people present
The safety of the space we’re entering
The cultural norms we should follow

When these models work, we feel calm and confident. Our predictions match reality, and we navigate the world smoothly. But when they fail—when the floorboards crack unexpectedly, or a friend acts strangely—we feel anxiety. Our internal model has been disrupted.
This moment of disruption is what storytellers call the Inciting Incident. The brain demands an explanation to bridge the gap between what it expected and what happened. It generates a “story” to regain control: “The floor is old,” “My friend is upset about something,” “I need to be careful here.”
This is not metaphor—this is cognitive architecture. The brain is literally constructing narrative explanations to maintain its sense of control over reality.


The Narrative Imperative
Consider this example: You’re scrolling through social media and notice that three different friends have posted about the same new app within 24 hours. Your brain immediately constructs explanatory narratives:

Story 1: “This app must be going viral.”
Story 2: “There’s probably an influencer campaign happening.”
Story 3: “Maybe there’s a new feature that solves a common problem.”

You haven’t analyzed data. You haven’t run statistics. Yet your brain has already generated three competing hypotheses to explain the pattern you observed. This is the storytelling mechanism at work—and it’s the foundation of scientific thinking.
The difference between casual observation and research is simply this: Research subjects these narrative explanations to systematic testing.

title: Chapter 1: The Science of Storytelling
text:
1.2 Research as Plot
Scientific inquiry follows the exact same structure as a compelling novel. We can map the components of a standard research study directly onto the components of a narrative arc:

The Story Structure of Science

1. The Inciting Incident → The Research Problem
The story begins with a gap in knowledge. You observe an anomaly in the media landscape that violates your expectations:

“Why is everyone suddenly watching chess on Twitch?”
“Why did that Super Bowl ad go viral when others didn’t?”
“Why are teen girls abandoning Instagram for BeReal?”

This violation of your expectations drives the plot forward. In academic writing, we call this the research problem or research question. In screenwriting, it’s the moment the protagonist’s normal world shatters.
Example: In March 2020, we noticed people flooding onto Twitch—not to watch esports professionals, but just to “hang out” in low-stakes streams. This didn’t match our model of Twitch as a gaming platform. That gap became our research question.


2. The Protagonist → The Researcher
This is you. You are the detective entering the unknown world to find the truth. Like any protagonist, you bring:

Skills: Your training in theory, methods, and critical thinking
Tools: Your research instruments (surveys, scrapers, interviews)
Motivation: Curiosity, career goals, or a desire to solve a real-world problem
Constraints: Time, budget, ethical boundaries

Your journey through the research process will change you. By the end, you’ll know something you didn’t know before—and that transformation is what makes you the protagonist.


3. The Antagonist → The Data
In research, the antagonist is not a villain, but chaos. It is:

The overwhelming noise of unorganized information
The difficulty of accessing data
The complexity of human behavior
The statistical variation that obscures patterns
The ethical and logistical barriers to perfect knowledge

Your goal is to defeat this chaos by organizing it. You impose structure on the formless through:

Coding schemes that categorize messy text
Variables that quantify complex phenomena
Statistical tests that separate signal from noise
Visualizations that reveal hidden patterns

The antagonist resists. Your sample is biased. Your coding is inconsistent. Your results are inconclusive. The plot thickens.


4. The Rising Action → Data Collection
Like any good story, research builds tension. You:

Design your study (plotting your path into the unknown)
Gain IRB approval (crossing the threshold)
Collect your data (venturing into the dark forest)
Encounter obstacles (participant dropout, API changes, messy data)

Each setback increases the stakes. Will you find the answer? Will the data support your hypothesis? The reader (or reviewer) leans forward.


5. The Climax → The Analysis
This is the moment of truth. You run your statistical test or finalize your coding. The tension breaks, and the answer is revealed:

“p < .05” — The relationship is significant!
“Kappa = .82” — The coding is reliable!
“r = .67” — The correlation is strong!

Or perhaps:

“p = .43” — No significant relationship found.
“The data was too noisy to draw conclusions.”

Even null findings tell a story. They tell us that the world is more complex than we thought—that our initial model needs refinement.


6. The Resolution → The Discussion
Like any story’s resolution, the Discussion section answers: “What does this mean?”

How does this finding change our understanding?
What are the implications for practitioners?
What should we study next?
How do we update our model of the world?

The protagonist (you) has transformed. You entered with a question; you exit with an answer (or a more sophisticated question).



Example: Mapping a Real Study
Let’s apply this to the Twitch study:








Story Element
Research Element
Our Example




Inciting Incident
Research Problem
People suddenly flocking to Twitch during quarantine


Protagonist
Researcher
SIM Lab team investigating streaming behavior


Antagonist
Data Chaos
Millions of chat messages, multiple languages, spam


Rising Action
Data Collection
Scraping 50,000+ chat logs from 200+ streams


Climax
Analysis
Statistical tests showing increased social/tension-release language


Resolution
Discussion
Twitch served as digital “third place” during isolation

title: Chapter 1: The Science of Storytelling
section: 1.3 The Sacred Flaw: The Null Hypothesis
text:
1.3 The Sacred Flaw: The Null Hypothesis
Perhaps the most powerful concept Storr offers is the “Sacred Flaw.” In fiction, a protagonist often clings to an erroneous belief about the world that protects their identity:

“I don’t need anyone” (Elsa in Frozen)
“Money equals happiness” (Charles Foster Kane in Citizen Kane)
“The past defines me” (Simba in The Lion King)

The plot forces them to confront this flaw. By the climax, they must abandon their false belief to achieve their goal.

The Null Hypothesis as Sacred Flaw
In science, we have a name for this Sacred Flaw: the Null Hypothesis (H₀).
The Null Hypothesis is the assumption that the world is boring and static—that there is no relationship between variables, no effect, and no change. It is the “flawed” model we currently accept as true until proven otherwise.
Examples:







Sacred Flaw (H₀)
The Story (H₁)




Violent video games have no effect on children
Actually, the data suggests they desensitize players to aggression


Social media usage is unrelated to anxiety
Actually, heavy use correlates with increased anxiety symptoms


Brand logos don’t influence purchasing
Actually, exposure to luxury logos triggers status-seeking behavior


Streaming is just entertainment
Actually, it serves social integration functions during isolation



Scientific inquiry is the process of exposing the Sacred Flaws in our collective understanding of media. We assume the current model (H₀) is true until the data becomes so overwhelming that we are forced to rewrite the story.


The Burden of Proof
Just as a fictional protagonist must earn their transformation through struggle, we cannot simply declare the Sacred Flaw false. We must:

State the null clearly: “There is no relationship between X and Y”
Collect rigorous evidence: Through valid, reliable methods
Test statistically: Is the pattern we see just random chance?
Reach a threshold: Typically p < .05 (less than 5% chance of randomness)
Only then reject H₀: And accept that the world is different than we thought

This is storytelling with stakes. We’re not just entertaining readers—we’re revising humanity’s collective understanding of reality.

title: Chapter 1: The Science of Storytelling
text:
1.4 Connecting Journalism to Data Science
If you can think like a journalist, you can act like a data scientist. Both professions share a single goal: to uncover the truth about the world. The difference lies only in the scale of the evidence.

The Journalist’s Toolkit
A journalist investigates a story by:

Observing: Noticing patterns in the world (e.g., “Everyone’s talking about this new app”)
Interviewing: Gathering firsthand accounts (e.g., “I spoke to 10 users who…”)
Contextualizing: Providing historical and cultural background
Synthesizing: Weaving observations into a coherent narrative

The journalist’s strength is depth. They can capture the texture of human experience—the fear in someone’s voice, the cultural nuance of a trend, the emotional weight of a moment.


The Data Scientist’s Toolkit
A data scientist investigates the same story by:

Observing: Noticing patterns in data (e.g., “App downloads increased 300%”)
Measuring: Gathering systematic evidence (e.g., “We tracked 10,000 users over 6 months”)
Modeling: Testing theoretical explanations statistically
Generalizing: Identifying patterns that apply beyond individual cases

The data scientist’s strength is breadth. They can detect patterns invisible to individual observation—the aggregate behavior of millions, the statistical correlation hidden in noise.


The Liaison’s Integration
You are learning to be both. You will:

Start with journalistic curiosity (What’s happening? Why does it matter?)
Gather systematic evidence (Let’s measure this at scale)
Analyze with statistical rigor (Is this pattern real or random?)
Communicate with narrative clarity (Here’s what this means for real people)

This is the power of the Communication Liaison: You speak both languages.

section: 1.5 Case Study: Twitch in the Time of Quarantine
text:
1.5 Case Study: Twitch in the Time of Quarantine
To illustrate this evolution from journalist to data scientist, let’s examine a study conducted at the SIM Lab: “Twitch in the Time of Quarantine” (Leith & Gheen, 2022).

Phase 1: The Journalist’s Observation
March 2020: As the COVID-19 lockdowns began, we noticed a massive cultural shift. Everyone we knew was suddenly logging onto Twitch—not just for gaming, but just to “hang out.” Streams with low production value and no competitive gameplay were getting thousands of viewers.
A journalist might write a think-piece titled: “How We Are Coping Online: The Rise of Parasocial Comfort in Digital Spaces.”
This is a valid observation. It’s culturally insightful. But it’s anecdotal—based on personal experience and limited interviews. A skeptical editor might ask:

“How do you know this is widespread?”
“Could you just be noticing it because you’re online more?”
“What’s the evidence beyond your friend group?”



Phase 2: The Scientist’s Inquiry
We took that observation and subjected it to the “Scientific Plot.”

The Inciting Incident (Research Problem)
Why are people flocking to a gaming site during a health crisis—especially people who aren’t gamers?


The Theory (Our Lens)
We applied Uses and Gratifications Theory (Katz, Blumler, & Gurevitch, 1974), which argues people use media to satisfy specific psychological needs:

Social Integrative needs: The need to belong, to feel connected
Tension Release needs: The need to escape, to relax

Our hypothesis: During quarantine, when in-person socializing became impossible, people turned to Twitch to satisfy these needs at scale.


The Investigation (Data Collection)
We scraped thousands of chat logs from Twitch streams spanning two time periods:

Pre-Pandemic: January–February 2020
During Pandemic: March–May 2020

We collected: - Chat volume (messages per minute) - Emotional sentiment (positive, negative, neutral) - Social language (greetings, gratitude, community references) - Content focus (game-related vs. off-topic conversation)


The Analysis (The Climax)
Using computational text analysis and statistical testing, we found:

Chat volume increased 47% during the pandemic
Social integrative language increased 31% (e.g., “miss you guys,” “feels good to be here”)
Tension-release expressions increased 28% (e.g., “need this right now,” “escaping reality”)
Off-topic conversation increased 19% (people talking about quarantine life, not games)

Statistical tests confirmed these increases were significant (p < .001), meaning there was less than a 0.1% chance they occurred randomly.


The Resolution (Discussion)
We moved from “vibes” (people seem lonely) to “variables” (a statistically significant rise in social integrative messaging).
Our conclusion: During COVID-19 lockdowns, Twitch functioned as a digital third place—a public space where people gathered not to consume content, but to simply be together in a shared experience.



What Changed?







Journalistic Approach
Scientific Approach




“People seem to be using Twitch differently”
“Chat volume increased 47% (p < .001)”


“It feels like a coping mechanism”
“Tension-release language up 28%”


“Based on my observations”
“Based on analysis of 50,000+ messages”


“This matters to me and my community”
“This generalizes to millions of users”



Both approaches are valuable. The journalist provides the soul (the human story). The scientist provides the spine (the empirical evidence).

title: Chapter 1: The Science of Storytelling
section: 1.6 Anecdote vs. Data: The Creative Tension
text:
1.6 Anecdote vs. Data: The Creative Tension
The “Journalist” in you collects anecdotes: specific, emotional stories about individuals.
Example: Interviewing one Twitch streamer about their anxiety during quarantine, hearing them describe crying during a stream when chat showed overwhelming support.
The “Scientist” in you collects data: the aggregation of thousands of anecdotes to prove a pattern.
Example: Counting how many streamers’ chats contained supportive language, correlating it with viewership retention, and testing whether this pattern held across different stream categories.

Neither Is Sufficient Alone
A white paper with only data is dry:

“Our analysis of 50,000 chat messages revealed a 31% increase in social integrative language (M = 4.2, SD = 1.7) compared to baseline (M = 3.2, SD = 1.4), t(498) = 7.84, p < .001.”

This is rigorous, but soulless. The reader’s eyes glaze over.
A white paper with only anecdotes is unproven:

“I spoke to Sarah, a streamer who told me she felt more connected to her audience during quarantine. She said, ‘It was like we were all going through this together.’ This shows how Twitch became a space for community during isolation.”

This is compelling, but unscientific. The reader wonders: “But is Sarah’s experience typical? Or just one person’s story?”


The Liaison’s Synthesis
The Publisher (you, by Week 17) uses both:

“During the COVID-19 lockdowns, Twitch emerged as a digital refuge. Sarah, a variety streamer from Ohio, described the shift: ‘It was like we were all going through this together.’ Our analysis of 50,000 chat messages confirms Sarah’s intuition was widespread—social integrative language increased 31% during quarantine (p < .001), suggesting millions of users turned to Twitch not just for entertainment, but for human connection.”

This synthesis: - Opens with context (the pandemic) - Introduces a human face (Sarah) - Uses her words (emotional resonance) - Validates with data (statistical evidence) - Explains significance (millions of users)
This is the power of combining journalism and data science. You’re not just reporting facts—you’re telling the truth in a way that moves people and withstands scrutiny.

title: Chapter 1: The Science of Storytelling
section: 1.7 The Research Mindset: From Consumer to Creator
text:
1.7 The Research Mindset: From Consumer to Creator
Most of your life, you’ve been a consumer of research: reading studies, citing sources, trusting experts. In this course, you become a creator of research: generating knowledge, testing theories, adding to the scholarly conversation.
This shift requires three mental transformations:

1. From Certainty to Curiosity
Old Mindset: “The answer is in the textbook. I just need to find it.”
New Mindset: “The answer doesn’t exist yet. I need to create it.”
Research is not about memorizing facts—it’s about generating new facts. You must become comfortable with uncertainty, ambiguity, and the possibility that your hypothesis is wrong.


2. From Description to Explanation
Old Mindset: “This is what happened.” (Reporting)
New Mindset: “This is why it happened.” (Analysis)
Description tells us what. Explanation tells us why. Theory provides the lens that transforms observation into insight.


3. From Opinion to Evidence
Old Mindset: “I think violent video games are harmful because they feel aggressive to me.”
New Mindset: “I hypothesize violent video games increase aggression. Let me design an experiment to test this claim against competing explanations.”
Opinions are starting points. Evidence is the destination. Research is the journey between them.

By default, community plugins are disabled. To enable them:

Click the Settings icon (gear icon) in the bottom left
Go to Community plugins
Click Turn on community plugins (if it’s greyed out, they’re already on)



4.2 Install a Plugin: QMD as Markdown
The textbook chapters are in .qmd format (Quarto markdown). Obsidian doesn’t recognize this format by default, but the qmd as md plugin fixes this.
To install it:

In Settings, go to Community plugins
Click Browse (or search icon)
Search for “qmd as md” (by Daniel Borek)
Click the result to open the plugin page
Click Install
Once installed, click Enable to turn it on

Now you can view and edit .qmd files just like regular markdown files!


4.3 Other Useful Plugins
Here are some community plugins that work great with the Liaison Program:







Plugin
What It Does




Dataview
Query and display your notes as databases/lists


Calendar
Visual calendar for journal entries


Templater
Advanced template features beyond Obsidian’s built-in system


Daily Notes
Automatically create and link daily notes


Task
Advanced task management with due dates and status


Excalidraw
Draw diagrams and sketches within notes



To install any of these, repeat steps 2-5 above with the plugin name.

title: Getting Started with Obsidian
text:
Step 5: Customize with Themes
Obsidian comes with a light and dark theme by default, but the community has created hundreds more. Here’s how to change themes.

5.1 Access Themes

Open Settings (gear icon, bottom left)
Go to Appearance
Scroll to Themes section



5.2 Choose a Built-in Theme
Under “Manage”, you’ll see two built-in themes: - Default Light Theme - Default Dark Theme (recommended for long study sessions)
Click either to apply it immediately.


5.3 Install Community Themes
For custom themes from the community:

Make sure community plugins are enabled (see Step 4.1)
In Appearance, look for Manage button next to Themes
Click Manage (or the folder icon)
Click Browse in the top right
Search for a theme name (e.g., “Minimal”, “Nord”, “Dracula”)
Click the theme to see a preview
Click Install and then Use



5.4 Popular Themes
Some community favorites:

Minimal - Clean, distraction-free interface
Nord - Cool blue color scheme, easy on the eyes
Dracula - Dark theme with vibrant accent colors
Cybertron - Modern, sleek design
Things - Inspired by the Things app, very polished

Try a few and find what works best for you!

title: Getting Started with Obsidian
text:
Step 6: Essential Settings

6.1 File Management
In Settings → Files & Links: - Default location for new notes: Choose where new notes appear (e.g., “Inbox” folder) - Show unsaved indicator: Helpful to know when to save


6.2 Editor Settings
In Settings → Editor: - Strict line breaks: Makes formatting more predictable - Line numbers: Toggle on/off based on preference - Indent size: Set to 2 or 4 spaces (2 is cleaner for markdown)


6.3 Hotkeys
In Settings → Hotkeys, you can set keyboard shortcuts for common actions: - Toggle sidebar (great for focus mode) - Create new note - Search in vault - Follow backlinks


6.4 Sync & Backup
In Settings → About, you’ll see sync options: - Obsidian Sync (paid): Cloud sync across devices - Git: Use Git to version control your vault (recommended for this course!) - Manual backups: Copy your vault folder regularly
For the Liaison Program, using Git is recommended so you can version control your work.

Step 8: Create Your First Note
Let’s practice:

Click the “Create new note” icon (top left, looks like a page)
Type a title like “My First Note”
Start writing in markdown:

# My First Note

## What I'm Learning

- Obsidian basics
- Markdown syntax
- How to organize my research

## Goals

1. Complete the Liaison Program
2. Master data analysis
3. Tell stories with data

Obsidian saves automatically—no need to click Save!
Notice the file appears in your vault in the File Explorer (left sidebar)

title: Getting Started with Obsidian
text:
Step 9: Connect Your Notes (Backlinks)
One powerful feature of Obsidian is linking notes together. This creates a “knowledge graph” of your research.

9.1 Create a Link
In any note, type [[ and start typing a note name:
# My Research

I'm reading [[Weekly Journal Template]] to understand the reflection process.

I also reference [[02_Literature]] for my sources.
Obsidian will suggest existing notes. Select one or type a new name to create a new linked note.


9.2 View Backlinks
On the right side of any note, you’ll see a Backlinks panel. This shows all notes that link to the current note—a powerful way to see connections in your research!

title: Getting Started with Obsidian
text:
Step 10: Tips for Success

Keep It Simple
Don’t over-customize at first. Start with the default theme and no plugins. Add what you need as you go.


Use the Vault Structure
The Liaison_Vault comes pre-organized: - 00_Inbox: Capture ideas quickly here - 01_Journal: Weekly reflections - 02_Literature: Research notes and citations - 03_Project: Your active research work - 04_Resources: Attach images, PDFs, videos
Follow this structure to stay organized.


Back Up Your Work
If using Git:
git add .
git commit -m "Update research notes"
git push
Or regularly copy your Liaison_Vault folder to an external drive.


Embrace Plain Text
One beauty of Obsidian is that everything is plain markdown. You can: - Open notes in any text editor - Version control with Git - Search with command-line tools - Never worry about proprietary formats

title: Getting Started with Obsidian
text:
Troubleshooting

QMD Files Won’t Open
Make sure you’ve installed and enabled the qmd as md plugin (see Step 4.2).


Plugin Not Showing
Try restarting Obsidian. Sometimes plugins need to reload.


Can’t Find My Vault
Make sure you opened the correct folder as a vault. Look for a .obsidian folder inside your vault folder—that’s how Obsidian knows it’s a vault.


Performance Slow
If Obsidian feels sluggish: - Disable unused plugins - Check your note count (very large vaults may slow down) - Restart Obsidian

title: Installing R & RStudio
text:
R and RStudio are essential tools for statistical analysis and data science in this course. This guide covers installation on all major operating systems.



R: The core statistical programming language and environment
RStudio: An IDE (Integrated Development Environment) that makes R much easier to use









Go to CRAN (Comprehensive R Archive Network)
Click “Download R for Windows”
Click “base” (first option)
Click the download link for the latest version (typically named something like R-4.x.x-win.exe)
Run the installer

Accept default settings (you can leave everything as-is)
Click through the installation wizard
Installation typically takes 2-5 minutes






Go to Posit RStudio Downloads
Click “Download RStudio Desktop” for Windows
Run the installer

Accept default settings
The installer will detect your R installation automatically
Complete the installation






Open RStudio (search for it in Windows Start menu)
In the Console pane (usually bottom-left), you should see something like:
R version 4.x.x (20XX-XX-XX) -- "..."
Type: print("Hello, R!") and press Enter
If you see [1] "Hello, R!", you’re ready to go!








Option A: Using the installer (Recommended for beginners)

Go to CRAN macOS
Click “Download R for macOS”
Select the appropriate version:

For Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3 chips): Download R-x.x.x-arm64.pkg
For Intel Macs: Download R-x.x.x-x86_64.pkg
(Unsure? Check Apple menu → About This Mac → Chip)

Run the .pkg installer and follow the prompts
Installation takes 2-5 minutes

Option B: Using Homebrew (if you use Homebrew)
brew install r




Go to Posit RStudio Downloads
Click “Download RStudio Desktop” for macOS
Select the appropriate version for your Mac (Apple Silicon or Intel)
Open the downloaded .dmg file
Drag RStudio to the Applications folder
Launch RStudio from Applications





Open RStudio (find in Applications folder or Spotlight search)
In the Console, type: print("Hello, R!") and press Enter
Confirm you see: [1] "Hello, R!"








# Update package lists
sudo apt update

# Install R
sudo apt install -y r-base r-base-dev




Go to Posit RStudio Downloads
Select “RStudio Desktop” → Choose Linux version (Ubuntu 20/22 or Debian)
Download the .deb file
Install it:
sudo dpkg -i rstudio-[version].deb

Or install from terminal directly:
sudo apt install -y rstudio




Launch RStudio from applications menu or terminal:
rstudio &
Test in Console: print("Hello, R!")
Confirm output: [1] "Hello, R!"







Once R and RStudio are installed, you need to set up your R environment for the course:


In RStudio Console, run:
setwd("~/Documents")  # Or your preferred workspace folder



We’ll use these packages throughout the course. Install them with:
# Core data science packages
install.packages(c(
  "tidyverse",      # Data wrangling and visualization
  "rmarkdown",      # Create documents with R code
  "quarto",         # Publishing system
  "shiny",          # Interactive web apps
  "ggplot2"         # Advanced visualization
))
This may take 5-15 minutes (packages are downloading and installing).



Test that the main packages work:
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
print("All packages loaded successfully!")
If no errors appear, you’re all set!








Windows: Try reinstalling R with administrator privileges
Mac: Restart your computer and try again
Linux: Run sudo apt install -y r-base to ensure all dependencies are installed





RStudio should auto-detect R, but if not:

Tools → Global Options → General
Look for “R version” section
If blank, manually browse to your R installation






Make sure you have internet connection
Try: install.packages("package_name", repos="http://cran.r-project.org")
Some packages require additional system libraries (ask in course chat!)





Try: install.packages("package", type="source")

Install a package
install.packages("package_name")


Get help
help(function_name) or ?function_name


Exit R
q()

RStudio Cheat Sheets: https://posit.co/resources/cheatsheets/

Course Support: Check the course discussion board for questions

Troubleshooting
Q: I extracted the ZIP file but Obsidian won’t open it as a vault - Make sure you’re opening the folder that contains the .obsidian hidden folder - Try right-clicking the folder and checking “Show hidden files” if needed
Q: Where do I put my weekly journal entries? - Create a new file in 01_Journal named something like Week_01_MyName.md - Copy the template from 99_Templates/Weekly_Journal_Template.md and fill it out
Q: Can I share my vault with classmates? - Yes! You can email them the ZIP file, or sync it via Git/GitHub for collaborative projects
